To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
diatoms can survive abrasive disturbance in crevices and that the size and shape of crevices influence the composition and size of the diatom community within crevices.

1) crevices can protect diatoms from abrasion; 2) diatom size and diversity are related to the size of crevice relative to organismal body size; 3) detritus can accumulate in crevices during abrasion, and can increase the protective effect of crevices; and 4) abrasion level can have a strong effect on algal communities in the absence of crevices, but a weak effect on communities within crevices.

1) diatom and filament algal densities were significantly greater on caddis fly cases than on all glass rods; 2) abrasion greatly reduced diatom and filament density; and 3) the small crevices on the sanded glass rods contained primarily A. minutissimum whereas the larger crevice on the scratched rods and cased caddis fly contained a greater range in diatom size and species diversity.
